A powering policy is a set of rules or an algorithm that determines what source of energy/power is used as the consist traverses the route. Currently, all policies maximize dynamic and regenerative braking. Fig. 1 Organization of the SCORE Toolset. There are three loops for optimization in the SCORE toolset. The first is used to determine an optimal locomotive configuration for a given route [1, 2, 3]. It is an outer loop optimization that requires an inner loop optimization of determining the optimal powering policy for the configuration and route. This becomes critical when incorporating regenerative capability (batteries) in the locomotive consist. There are routes, for example, where an optimal policy may require a diesel locomotive to provide excess power to the rail that is then consumed by the battery, ensuring sufficient energy available to power up a steep grade further along the route. There is a second outer loop that can explore the robustness of a single consist configuration over multiple routes or examine a portfolio of multiple routes and consists. The remainder of this paper defines the problem being solved by the SCORE toolset. Next the algorithms used in the E-LTD and optimal powering policy are presented along with assumptions and constraints. The E-LTD incorporating the algorithm is run against a series of test cases to demonstrate its efficacy. The paper concludes with future work to expand capability. II. Problem Definition The Department of Energy (DOE) needs a comprehensive set of open-source tools tailored to the modeling of energy trade studies that can be provided to industry and organizations developing advanced energy solutions to evaluate their efficacy in the context of a transportation system. Yet open-source software tools do not exist to explore and evaluate advanced energy and power technologies that can reduce environmental impacts at an acceptable cost to industry. Current data for rail lines, locomotives, and rail cars is industry owned and controlled, hindering access to historical costs, emissions, and traffic. The next three sections describe the route generation, consist generation, and the E-LTD toolsets developed for and used by SCORE. A. Route Generation Toolset 3 Rail network data exists in the public domain, e.g., DOT and OpenRailwayMap†† databases, but these sources lack elevation and curvature information and do not identify routes operating over the network. As a result, we use the North American Railway Network (NARN) database‡‡ as a source for our network lines. This database includes latitude and longitude points and length (in miles) for the railway lines in addition to meta data including ownership, track rights, and type (e.g., mainline, siding, or yard). Geopandas is a Python-based GIS library used to explore, manipulate, and manage the railway data. Using Geopandas, it is simple to convert from the original “4326” coordinate reference system (CRS) that uses units of degrees for lat/long to the “3857” CRS that maps those points to meters.
